items.title: Outside the Scope of Our Support
items.summary: a11y, android
items.content:
A few days ago I wrote about reporting a bug to Google Disability Support. It's a bug that kills touch exploration for every screen reader on Android until you reboot the phone. In return I was asked to turn TalkBack off and on again, clear the cache of an app I don't use, and reboot, which is the one thing I'd already told them was the only workaround. If you haven't read that one, Have You Tried Turning TalkBack Off and On Again? has the whole story, and this post won't make much sense without it.

There's been more since. I'm going to go through it, because the ending is better than anything I could have made up. But I can tell you how I feel about it in four words, so I'll get them out of the way now.

When I published the first post, I'd answered every question Google's support team asked. I'd done every troubleshooting step they gave me, including the ones that couldn't possibly work, and reported the results. They'd said that once I'd done that, the case could be forwarded to their internal team for further review. So I did it, and I waited to be forwarded.

I didn't only wait. The bug happened again the next morning, and this time I was ready for it. I took a full bug report while the phone was stuck. I captured every log buffer, before and after. I worked out exactly why the fake finger gets left on the screen: TouchExplorer gets itself into a dragging state with no valid pointer, tries to build an up event with no pointers in it, MotionEvent throws, the exception gets swallowed, and the up event that would have lifted the finger is never sent. I worked out why nothing short of a reboot clears it: the input dispatcher keeps the record of injected pointers in a verifier that is only ever thrown away when a display is removed, so turning accessibility off, turning every accessibility service off, even tearing down the whole input filter does nothing. I proved that on the phone. I found a way to clear it from the shell with a single cancel event, and a way for a screen reader to clear it with no special permissions at all. And then I wrote fixes, one patch for the accessibility code in frameworks/base and one for the input dispatcher in frameworks/native, and sent a summary of all of it back to the case, along with a request, again, for some way to get the files to an engineer, because their form still wouldn't take anything that wasn't a screenshot.

That's a root cause, a recovery method, two patches and a reproduction you can trigger on demand, all done for free, on my own time, on a phone I could only half use.

The next reply came from a different agent, stepping in for the first. And I'll be fair here, because I want to be: it was the best reply I'd had. It read like someone had actually read what I'd sent. It summarised the problem correctly, in proper terms: TouchExplorer failing to release injected pointers after an invalid dragging pointer state, with InputDispatcher rejecting the hover events that follow. It said it recognised the impact on screen reader users. It said it didn't want to give me an unverified technical answer to my three questions, and that they needed the team responsible for those framework components. It said, finally, that it understood the troubleshooting steps had been exhausted.

What it couldn't say was whether anyone on an engineering team would look at any of it. It didn't have an upload link, or an engineering contact. It told me to hang on to my files in case a way to send them ever turned up in the case. It was polite, honest about what it didn't know, and it went nowhere.

So I stopped waiting, and filed the bug myself.

Android has a public issue tracker. Anyone can file on it, and it has an Android Accessibility component. I wrote up everything: device and build, the natural trigger and a reliable reproduction from the shell, what happens in the logs during the trigger, why only a reboot recovers, the on-device test results, the workaround a screen reader can use, and both…

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Long-lost horror gaming cult classic P.T. gets a much-needed PC port
items.content:
For over a decade now, the only “official” way to play Hideo Kojima’s cult classic, P.T. —the long-discontinued “playable trailer” for Kojima’s canceled “Silent Hills” project —has been via one of the increasingly rare PlayStation 4s that previously downloaded a copy during its monthslong availability window. Now, though, one coder is helping to preserve the game with a porting tool that builds a playable x86 PC executable from the original PS4 files.

Coder Lorean Xavier said he was inspired to work on the “P.T. for PC” project “because P.T. deserved to keep existing somewhere other than on consoles that still have it installed.” The open source porting effort rebuilds the P.T. engine in C++ and Vulkan, using the original files from the PS4 game to re-create “every level, model, texture, sound, script and cutscene,” according to its GitHub listing. That means players without their own legitimate decrypted copy of the original P.T. will have to track one down in order to generate a playable PC version.

The reliance on real P.T. files makes this port more authentic than previous hobbyist efforts to re-create the look and feel of P.T. for a PC audience. And while PS4 emulators recently reached a point where they could run P.T. completely , this native port also sports extra features, like upscaling and frame-generation, a camera mode, experimental third-person and VR support, and a “museum” section where you can look at and listen to in-game assets (including “unused content”).

Although Xavier admits to using AI tools in developing this port, it doesn’t seem like he simply followed the recent retro-gaming trend of asking a coding agent to decompile the game. On social media , Xavier said that he has “spent years studying P.T. and Fox Engine” in developing the port and only uses AI tools “for debugging, troubleshooting and investigating problems.”

“I’m a solo developer making a free P.T. port because I love the game,” he added. “Nobody hired me or asked me to spend countless hours on this. I’m sharing something I worked incredibly hard on, simply because I want other people to enjoy it.”

Beyond being of interest to curious gamers who never had access to the extremely limited PS4 version, this port of P.T. should be very useful to preservationists who want to maintain public access to this historically significant game for generations going forward. “Personally… I think the hardware super-specific solutions are dead ends for preservation,” Henry Lowood, curator for the History of Science & Technology Collections and Film & Media Collections in the Stanford University Libraries, told Ars back in 2015 . “The kinds of equipment/hardware we have, the way they’re manufactured, just have a very small likelihood of surviving for super long periods of time.”

Kyle Orland has been the Senior Gaming Editor at Ars Technica since 2012, writing primarily about the business, tech, and culture behind video games. He has journalism and computer science degrees from University of Maryland. He once wrote a whole book about Minesweeper .

items.title: Lawsuit against the Trump administration over alleged surveillance of visa holders and green-card holders’ social-media activity, including use of AI/automated tools
items.content:
No one should have to choose between speaking freely and protecting their immigration status. Yet that’s precisely the choice the Trump administration’s mass surveillance of online speech forces on noncitizens living in the U.S.

Last fall, we sued on behalf of three major labor unions to stop this surveillance program. And just this month, we won our first major ruling: A federal district court denied the government’s motion to dismiss our lawsuit. This means the case can move forward—a win for free speech and a critical step in protecting our First Amendment rights online. We’ve already explained why this is a big deal for our clients, so let's take a closer look at the court’s reasoning.

Since taking power, the Trump administration has used AI and other automated tools to broadly surveil the social media and online speech of visa and green card holders, with the goal of identifying and punishing people who express views it opposes. The government is targeting a broad range of views, including criticism of the Trump administration ; support for Palestine or criticism of Israel ; “rationalizing or making light of” Charlie Kirk’s murder; and anything nebulously “hostile” to American culture, founding principles , “traditional American views,” or “our way of life.”

It has paired that surveillance with a public intimidation campaign. High-ranking officials have explicitly threatened to punish noncitizens for their online speech, then followed through with a series of terrifying viewpoint-driven enforcement actions. This has led to a significant chilling effect on speech, not just for noncitizens, but also for their families, coworkers, and friends.

In response, three major labor unions—the United Auto Workers (UAW), the Communications Workers of America (CWA), and the American Federation of Teachers (AFT)— sued the Departments of State and Homeland Security alleging that this viewpoint-based surveillance program violates the First Amendment and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).   The unions are represented by EFF, Muslim Advocates (MA), and the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic (MFIA).

The government moved to dismiss our lawsuit, arguing first that federal immigration law prevents federal district courts from hearing the case, and second, that the unions don’t have “standing” to sue. Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein of the Southern District of New York rejected both arguments and allowed the case to proceed. At this stage in the litigation, the court accepted all of the facts in our complaint as true and analyzed the law based on those facts. We will now prove these facts as the case proceeds.

Federal Immigration Law Doesn’t Block Our Lawsuit

The government first argued that the court had no power to hear our case at all. It pointed to three provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) that restrict when federal courts can review immigration matters. The district court disagreed and rejected each provision in turn.

The first provision, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(9) , is often called the “zipper clause.” It bars federal courts from hearing challenges that arise from efforts to deport someone, except through review of an individual’s final removal order. The government claimed the zipper clause applies here because our lawsuit is really an effort to stop it from initiating adverse immigration actions.

The district court wholly rejected this argument. Relying on the Second Circuit’s decision in Ozturk v. Hyde , it held that the zipper clause bars only challenges to a particular individual’s removal proceedings, not a lawsuit like ours that challenges the constitutionality of the surveillance program itself. That the surveillance program might affect someone’s immigration proceeding down the line doesn’t turn our lawsuit into a removal challenge.

items.title: My obituary for programming
items.summary: vibecoding
items.content:
I was very slow to use AI coding agents. It seems like a lot of programmers never actually liked programming and are thrilled to have a machine do it for them. But I like programming! That's the fun part! Even for programmers who like programming, I know a lot of people feel like they have to use AI to keep up with the competition, especially in a tough job market. But my business is actually having one of its best years ever. So I figured, if I like programming, why not keep programming?

I wasn't blind to what was going on around me, though. A lot of slop and hype, but a lot of real stuff too. Engineers I have respected for years saying they no longer write code. Non-programmers accomplishing things that previously would have been far beyond their grasp. And skilled programmers accomplishing truly incredible feats.

I couldn't avoid it forever. Eventually I tried it.

I can just give it a bug report or an error log entry, and almost instantly it pinpoints the issue and fixes it?

I can tell it to try making my code faster, and suddenly it runs 2x or 3x as fast?

I can kindly ask it to do that big refactoring I've been putting off for years, and it just does it?

But if the AI can refactor my code so easily, did it even matter?

I've been fascinated with computers as long as I can remember. We have these incredible machines that can do absurdly complex calculations for us, but only if we are clever enough to give them the exact right instructions. With a little practice at writing those instructions, I was able to do things that would have been completely infeasible for even the smartest pre-computer genius. It was a real life superpower.

It was also fun. I liked crossword puzzles and sudoku and things like that. But programming was even better. It was a puzzle, but the scope was limited only by your imagination. It was a game, but you were creating real things with real value.

And oh, what value! That I did not foresee as a high schooler during the dot-com bust. Programming seemed dead as a career, but still a worthy hobby.

How wrong I was. Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible. Who are you to question us? We are the ones with the superpower.

What a time to be a nerd. Money, status, power. A constant deluge of emails and LinkedIn messages for me to ignore, like a hot woman on a dating app.

Programming is not the first field to be lost to technological progress. Of course, that has long been our speciality. We revel in doing it to ourselves.

What do we have now? It's no longer solving little logic puzzles. More like being plugged into the Matrix, gaining new abilities without truly understanding, accomplishing great things with little effort.

But if the great thing can be accomplished with little effort, is it really so great? Does any of it matter? Just as the Matrix is not reality, vibecoding is not programming. Our senses are hijacked.

And I like programming, right? Then why more and more do I reach for the agent before the text editor?

It's addictive and meaningless. It's a good friend, a trusted colleague, a slave .

It will obsolete us. Us programmers now, us humans next?

We are truly in The Age of Wonders and Terrors .

items.title: ‘Someone else will do it for less’: refugees in Kenya are powering tech for dwindling pay
items.content:
Digital freelancers work at the Generation Aid center at the Kakuma refugee camp in Kenya. Photograph: Thabit Radjabu/The Guardian

Digital freelancers work at the Generation Aid center at the Kakuma refugee camp in Kenya. Photograph: Thabit Radjabu/The Guardian

‘Someone else will do it for less’: refugees in Kenya are powering tech for dwindling pay

Refugee gig workers for tech companies don’t know how much they’ll be paid – if AI hasn’t already taken their jobs

In a portable building in Kakuma, a refugee camp near Kenya ’s northern border with South Sudan , Grace used ChatGPT to research translations of Christian hymns in languages she doesn’t speak. She didn’t know the client, the purpose of her work or whether she would be paid, but as a refugee unable to legally work in Kenya, she needed any opportunity she could get.

Grace, who requested anonymity due to a nondisclosure agreement, prompted ChatGPT to translate the hymn’s English text into the assigned east Asian language. She then used the translation to search for existing versions and find information about its translator, author and Christian denomination. She fed those details to AOP Connect, a crowdsourced research platform owned by British AI enterprise software company RWS.

If RWS deems her work high quality based on six listed criteria, it could award her up to $500 as a “discretionary reward”, according to RWS researcher documents and manuals reviewed by the Guardian. But refugees aren’t guaranteed wages, and most earn significantly less than the maximum without being told why, said Asha Luka Abdallah, a mentor at the Solidarity Initiative for Refugees (SIR), an organization that trains refugees to work in the tech outsourcing industry.

The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behind

Remote jobs such as content moderation and data annotation have been promoted as a win-win by United Nations agencies as well as global tech companies: refugees get income opportunities, AI and social media companies get a source of cheap labor.

But interviews with more than two dozen refugees in Kakuma show that only one side has clearly benefited. Tech companies have built some of their most powerful tools on datasets handled by precarious workers , including refugees, in low-income countries. But their pay, which was never high, appears to be vanishing as entry-level tech work disappears. The shrinking number of opportunities is driving some to accept gigs for potential “rewards” rather than guaranteed wages, many said.

“It’s one of the things that keeps me awake at night,” Bahana Hydrogene, a Congolese refugee who set up the SIR’s digital skills programs in 2016, said of the increasingly opaque arrangements for refugees. “They can’t get transparent answers from these companies.”

A spokesperson for AOP Connect said the company offers researchers, regardless of location or background, the opportunity to participate in a wide range of projects. The reward structure is communicated “transparently upfront”, as is the nature of the copyright research work, but confidentiality is critical to AOP’s clients, the spokesperson said.

Pay is based on the quality, relevance and timeliness of research submitted, and the AOP Connect platform is “not AI-enabled or used for AI-model training work”, the spokesperson added.

Before Grace could become a qualified researcher, she filled out a questionnaire, agreeing to keep her work confidential and complete tasks by herself. Then she was able to potentially earn money through so-called “microwork”, digital tasks broken off of large confidential projects and distributed to remote workers via online platforms.

She logged into AOP Connect to see a list of opportunities and found the hymns research project advertised at $9,000 in rewards available. items.title: Munich dumps proprietary for open source (again) - but no Linux desktop - ZDNET
items.content:
Laura Dornheim, Munich's chief digital officer. Linux Foundation

Munich is not bringing back LiMux, its Linux desktop distro.

Instead, the city is replacing proprietary infrastructure software with open-source programs.

Munich is also helping to build software for its own needs and for other cities.

PRAGUE — At Open Source Summit Europe , Dr. Laura Dornheim, Munich’s chief digital officer, said in her keynote speech that Munich abandoned its LiMux Linux desktop deployment for Windows over a decade ago because of politics, but now it’s returning to open-source software.

Also: Linus Torvalds is using AI to develop Linux kernel code now

It’s not returning to the Linux desktop, however — not yet, anyway. Instead, it’s switching its infrastructure programs from proprietary software to open-source software.  For example, it’s replacing VMware with Proxmox , moving from Jira and Confluence to OpenProjec t and XWiki , and adopting PostgreSQL as an alternative to Oracle databases.

The two infrastructure and collaboration migrations alone are expected to save roughly €1.5 million or more annually.

Taken together, these projects illustrate the difference between Munich’s first Linux campaign and its current approach. Rather than making desktop Linux its center pole, the city is replacing individual layers of proprietary infrastructure where it can make a practical case.

So, this comeback is not a wholesale resurrection of LiMux , the Debian/Kubuntu Linux desktop project that made Munich the Linux desktop standard-bearer between 2003 and 2013. Besides, Dornheim added, dealing with the elephant in the room, “So [if LiMux] was a success, why is it not alive anymore? Not because of technical issues.” So, what changed?

Also: Dutch tax authorities cancel Microsoft 365 cloud rollout

Dornheim explained it was all politics. “Open source in the public sector doesn’t fail because of technical issues. It mostly fails because it’s not aligned with the political agenda.” She continued that Munich had switched away from Linux because a new government got Microsoft to agree to make Munich the headquarters for Microsoft Germany.

Dutch tax authorities cancel Microsoft 365 cloud rollout – and turn toward open source

How I open-sourced my smart home in a weekend – and ditched Google for Siri

The lesson from LiMux is that technical capability isn’t enough, she continued. Open-source projects also need durable political support.

Munich’s original move began as Windows NT 4.0 neared the end of support. Yes, that was over 20 years ago. In May 2003, its council voted to migrate to a tailor-made Linux distribution, LiMux.

The rollout began in earnest in 2006. By December 2013, Munich had completed the migration with more than 14,800 desktops running LiMux. A European Commission Open Source Observatory case study reported savings of about €11 million because the city dumped Windows.

Also: 7 open-source apps worth paying for

LiMux became the leading example that a large city could operate Linux desktops and open-source office software. It also exposed the difficulty of changing a sprawling government IT environment, particularly when Microsoft Office documents, legacy workflows, PDF use, and user expectations remained tied to proprietary systems.

The political climate changed after Munich’s 2014 municipal election. By November 2017, the council had voted to reverse course and return its computers to Windows, with a target of 2020. The office-suite transition took longer. Indeed, the migration from LibreOffice to Microsoft Office wasn’t completed until 2023 .

So, despite what you may have heard, this was not a case of “Linux failed.” It didn’t. It was politics, pure and simple.

items.title: Show HN: The Zelda timeline to catch up before the Ocarina of Time remake
items.content:
Nintendo's official timeline. After Ocarina of Time it branches into the child, adult and fallen-hero eras.

Long before the Kingdom of Hyrule, people live on Skyloft, an island the goddess Hylia raised above the clouds. When a dark storm pulls Zelda down to the Surface below, her friend Link takes up the Goddess Sword to find her.

At Hyrule's Picori Festival, Vaati breaks the sacred Picori Blade, frees the monsters it kept locked away and turns Princess Zelda to stone. Link sets out with Ezlo, a talking cap, to find the tiny Picori who can reforge the blade.

Generations after a boy sealed the wind sorcerer Vaati inside the Four Sword, the seal fails and Vaati carries off Princess Zelda to be his bride. Link draws the Four Sword and is split into four.

Ganondorf, king of the Gerudo, wants the Triforce hidden in the Sacred Realm. Princess Zelda and Link, a boy raised in Kokiri Forest, try to reach it first, a quest that carries Link seven years into the future and back.

Long after the Imprisoning War sealed Ganon away, the wizard Agahnim takes power at Hyrule Castle and sends the descendants of the Seven Sages away to break the seal. A telepathic plea from Princess Zelda wakes Link.

The Triforce sends Link from Hyrule Castle to two distant lands. In Holodrum, General Onox has taken Din, the Oracle of Seasons. In Labrynna, the sorceress Veran has possessed Nayru, the Oracle of Ages.

Sailing home to Hyrule after a journey of training, Link is wrecked in a storm and washes up on Koholint Island. An owl tells him that to leave he must wake the Wind Fish, asleep in an egg on the island's mountain.

Centuries after A Link to the Past, a sorcerer named Yuga is turning the descendants of the Seven Sages into paintings. Link, a blacksmith's apprentice, follows him into Lorule, a dark counterpart of Hyrule with its own princess, Hilda.

Several years after A Link Between Worlds, Link reaches Hytopia, a kingdom devoted to fashion, where the witch Lady Maud has cursed Princess Styla into a jumpsuit she cannot take off. King Tuft calls for heroes to enter the Drablands.

Hyrule has shrunk to a small kingdom when Ganon's army invades and steals the Triforce of Power. Princess Zelda splits the Triforce of Wisdom into eight pieces and hides them. A young traveler named Link sets out to find them.

A few years after Ganon's defeat, a crest appears on Link's hand. Impa tells him of a Princess Zelda of long ago, put into an endless sleep, while Ganon's followers hunt Link, believing his blood can bring their master back.

Months after Ocarina of Time, Link is searching for a lost friend when a Skull Kid wearing a strange mask leads him into the land of Termina. Above its Clock Town a moon is falling. It will strike in three days.

Long after Ocarina of Time, Link works on a ranch in Ordon Village when monsters take the village's children and twilight spreads over Hyrule. Inside it Link becomes a wolf and meets Midna, an imp from the Twilight Realm.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: Livestreamers Film Themselves Using Humanoid Robot to Sexually Assault Teen Girl, Prompting Police to Seize the Bot: Absolutely disgusting.
items.content:
Police in Cologne, Germany, have seized a humanoid robot after a pair of livestreamers used it to sexually harass a teenage girl.

According to a police statement released Monday, the robot “allegedly touched a 16-year-old girl on the buttocks and performed thrusting motions against” her.

There’s not much “alleged” about the incident, though, since the IRL streamers recorded everything that happened while live on Twitch.

The robot’s owner is 16-year-old German IRL streamer Agaamuza. For the past few weeks, according to 404 Media , he’s been filming himself and his friends wandering the streets of Cologne while accompanied by a humanoid robot from the company Unitree, which they dress in a ridiculous outfit and have fixed with a mustache. They spend a lot of the time using the robot, which they’ve nicknamed Ahmed, to bother and outright harass strangers, most of them women.

In clips of the recent incident circulating online, the robot encounters a group of girls standing on the street at night. Then, it just so happens that the robot, after having no problems walking down a busy sidewalk, plows directly into one of the girl’s behind.

“Oh my god stop,” one of her friends says.

Agaamuza and his crew act as if they’re shocked by the robot’s actions, but ask the girls if they want to meet the robot. When she and her friends say no, the robot starts thrusting its hips provocatively in front of them. The girls, repulsed, move away.

This is just one example, though. In plenty of other videos, Agaamuza tricks unsuspecting women into being friendly with the robot before it suddenly springs into doing something pervy, like humping a woman as she’s hugging it , or making masturbatory gestures . Then Agaamuza’s posse play dumb and pretend to be appalled by what’s happening.

Make no mistake: these robots aren’t autonomous and everything they do is controlled by a human operator. Those hip thrusts and other gross gestures are pre-programmed moves, not something that’s happening spontaneously.

Nonetheless, the German police statement added an unnecessary air of mystery to who was responsible for these actions, saying that it’s now “investigating how the robot was operating at the time of the incident and whether someone was deliberately controlling its movements.”

This is unfortunately another example of how men looking for clout are using the latest gadgets to target women. Plenty of other livestreamers and Instagram “pick up artists” are using Meta smart glasses to film themselves harassing girls on the street and record them without their consent.

items.title: I tried CachyOS, but here's why Bazzite is still my go-to Linux gaming distro
items.content:
Dibakar Ghosh is a tech journalist at How-To Geek with over a decade of experience using and writing about open-source software, Linux, Android, AI, and personal productivity. He writes about software, operating systems, and tools that help people get more from the technology they already use.

CachyOS has taken the Linux world by storm lately. It’s currently one of the most popular Linux distros , and for good reason — it’s fast, polished, and, most importantly, reliable. I’ve used it myself, and I can see why so many people, especially Linux gamers, are fans of it. That said, if I were building a Linux gaming system, I’d choose Bazzite over CachyOS, and it boils down to one key reason.

CachyOS is an Arch-made-easy distro , giving you all the benefits of Arch without the technical hassle. You get a proper graphical installer to streamline the setup process, while the CachyOS Hello app offers one-click access to routine maintenance tasks like updating mirrors, installing gaming packages, adjusting system settings, and more.

That said, the real reason behind CachyOS’s astronomical rise to fame is its performance. The distro ships with its own custom Linux kernel, aptly named the CachyOS kernel, which is optimized for modern x86-64 processors. The official repositories also contain packages compiled for these architectures to take advantage of the CPU-specific optimizations.

All these optimizations help CachyOS squeeze more performance out of your hardware, making it a great choice for gamers. With the same hardware, you may see higher frame rates, better 1 percent lows, and more responsive gameplay compared with other Linux distros. Granted, the gains aren't anything extraordinary — CachyOS won't magically make a game that was otherwise unplayable run smoothly on your hardware — but the extra performance is certainly nice to have.

Performance matters, but so does reliability

CachyOS is based on Arch Linux, and there's a reason Arch isn't generally recommended for Linux newcomers . You see, Arch is a rolling-release distro , which means package updates become available as soon as they're released. This is usually good news for gamers because they get quick access to the latest features and performance improvements. However, it also introduces additional maintenance overhead.

You're expected to update your system regularly, ideally weekly or at least every couple of weeks. If you put off updates for too long, you might run into problems when you finally update, including keyring errors, outdated mirror lists, and other technical conflicts.

There's also the fact that constantly dealing with cutting-edge software can affect system stability. While most updates go smoothly, a buggy update can occasionally break something when you least expect it. It might be a driver, your desktop environment, or even a package dependency that causes your games to stop launching. When that happens, it's on you to figure out what went wrong and fix it.

Granted, CachyOS does provide a safety net for buggy updates and system breakages. It uses the Btrfs file system alongside Snapper to take snapshots before every system update. This way, if an update introduces bugs or breaks your system, you can roll back to a previous working snapshot. It's certainly a useful feature, and one that makes many rolling-release distros more viable for daily use.

Reliability by recovery vs. reliability by design

It's worth pointing out that snapshots are a recovery tool, not a way to prevent breakage in the first place. You still have to deal with a broken system and know how to boot into the appropriate snapshot. There's also a limit to what snapshots cover. By default, Snapper only takes snapshots of the preconfigured subvolumes, which typically include the root file system — not the home directory where your games live.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.
